newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban hold sports parade in Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Taleban hold sports parade in Kabul.

text.p: The purist Islamic Taleban organised a parade of sports teams in a stadium in Kabul on Tuesday to celebrate their victory over the ousted government and to prove that they were not against sports.

"When we organised this parade we had two intentions. First to celebrate the takeover of Kabul, and secondly to show that we are not against sport," Abdul Shukur Motmayn, the Taleban-appointed head of the Olympic committee told Reuters on Tuesday morning.

"Whenever we conquer a province, I get an order from the Amir-al-Momineen (Leader of the Faithful -- a title given by the Taleban to their leader Mullah Mohammed Omar) to organise such a demonstration to reassure athletes who have panicked because they think that the Taleban have banned sport."

"Also, if we have opposition to sports among the ranks of the Taleban, we hope it will be overcome by the participation of senior Taleban leaders in the Parade," said Motmayn. He said there was no truth in reports that the Taleban had banned or intended to ban sports.

Tuesday's parade was attended by the deputy foreign minister and the minister of information and culture. Teams paraded in front of the assembled dignitaries to the muted sound of chanted verses of the Islamic holy text, the Koran.
A commentator introduced the teams, interspersing his commentary with improving statements: "Of all the disciplines, the best is the discipline of Shariat (Islamic Law)," he said.
Motmayn said that sportsmen in Afghanistan would have to abide by the Taleban's strict interpretation of Islamic Law.
"Shariat does not allow short sleeves or short trousers," he said.
He explained that some of teams that appeared at the parade in short sleeves could not afford to buy new uniforms. The soccer players wore shorts over tracksuit trousers.
"In future the dress of all players in local matches and exhibitions will have to conform to Sharia," he said. However, Motmayn said that an exception would be made where foreign teams were involved.
"If the teams go abroad, or if foreign teams come to Afghanistan, neither team will be forced to wear long sleeves or trousers," he said.

A broad range of sports was represented at the parade. Besides football, there were representatives from boxing, wrestling, martial arts, hockey, tennis, cycling, baseball, basketball and table tennis.
Motmayn said Afghanistan did not have a shooting team, although there were plenty of men armed with grenade launchers, machine guns and Kalashnikov rifles at the parade.
All participants were male, but Motmayn said the Taleban were not against women competing when the time is right.

"In the future, women will be allowed to compete. Now we are in an emergency situation and we cannot allow them to take part. When we have security, women will be allowed to take part in competitions," said Motmayn.
